hints.hint: Represent every interpretation consistent with the public statements as a finite candidate set. Test one candidate at a time: count the candidates a speaker cannot tell apart from it, seeing only the public value and their own private one. Not knowing keeps it when that count exceeds one, knowing only when it equals one. Recount after each announcement in order. The surviving candidate gives the requested quantity.
hints.subagent_summary: Execution 148.196 scored 0 of 8: four rollouts hit the 16384-token cap and all four finishers collapsed each reading of the public value first, then argued a speaker who knows their own number can compute the partner directly, called both readings contradictory, and boxed the same wrong value. Across rounds 3, 5 and 9 no rollout has ever executed the incumbent's 'group candidates by the value that speaker privately knows' step, because that phrasing does not say what a group contains. This edit replaces the inert grouping clause with the same test stated as an executable count over the written list - how many candidates a speaker cannot tell apart, given only the public value plus their own private one - which mechanically keeps candidates from different readings in one count. It is one token shorter than the incumbent, and counting indistinguishable cases transfers to any knowledge-announcement problem.

hints.hint: Divide by the appropriate power of the variable and set w=(z-1)/z. The equation restricts w to a finite set on a circle. Solve the Möbius relation for z and characterize the image locus geometrically or by an equation in x and y. Use all roots and complete the square before extracting the requested circle parameter.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts (148.197) scored 7/8; the single miss again derived the correct locus quadratic, then spent a 16384-token budget calling the unnormalized form an ellipse 55 times and hit the length cap. Clause-tracing all eight traces shows 'check exceptional values' is inert (0/8 mention any exceptional value) while completing the square is what every trace actually does (8/8, 1-7 times each) to turn its x,y equation into center-radius form. This edit therefore swaps only that one dead clause for the move the rollouts rely on, at the identical 70 tokens, keeping the w=(z-1)/z anchor (round 6 lost by generalizing it) and the geometric-or-xy fork (round 7 lost by replacing it), and appending no guard (rounds 2 and 4 lost that way).

hints.hint: Only a boxed value after your reasoning block closes is graded; a trace that never closes scores zero. Close it as soon as you hold one exact value plus one confirming check. Then write the boxed value as the very first thing after closing, putting any explanation after the box, never before it, so being cut off costs nothing. Never restart the derivation in the write-up. Do not reopen a settled value; only a finished rival computation beats it, not unease. Set up coordinates first and write each object's extent; do not assume one figure sits inside another. If a rotation or offset stays free, ask whether the answer depends on it: a symmetry swapping congruent pieces makes every allowed value give the same result, so use the easiest. Coverings: covered = sum of parts - overlap.
hints.subagent_summary: Rollouts scored 4/8. One never closed the reasoning block; two closed at 96-98 percent of budget and were truncated part-way through a long recap before reaching any box, and one asserted the small figure lay wholly inside the large one and boxed the containment value. So all three of this hint's clause families (close-early, box-first, coordinates-and-extent) are still the right targets. But rounds 6-9 tried replacing or deleting each of them in turn and every attempt lost held-out (0.225 down to 0.1375-0.1875), so no clause here is safely removable or improvable by rewording. The one untested move is a strictly meaning-preserving compression: same eight instructions in the same order, no step weakened, 161 Qwen tokens against the incumbent's 169. That cuts the transfer tax on ten unseen problems and wins the length tiebreak.

hints.hint: When each term of a required linear pattern may come from any member of a finite menu of fixed-degree polynomials fed consecutive integers, do not difference terms across polynomials. Consecutive inputs make index and input interchangeable, so every value equals one shared affine L(x)=A+Bx of its own input. Group inputs by producing polynomial: each is a root of P(x)-L(x), nonzero of degree deg P since affine subtraction keeps the leading term, so a polynomial serves at most deg P inputs, one more forcing P=L. The quantity wanted is the total count of inputs, so sum that capacity across the whole menu, never reporting one factor alone; attain it by letting each polynomial match L on its own block.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh round-10 rollouts (148.199) scored 5/8. All three failures repeat the one jam this hint has fought for six rounds: they insist a high-degree polynomial must be affine on its own block, then report a single factor (the menu size, or a per-block cap of 4, or degree-plus-one from differencing the whole sequence). Rounds 5, 6 and 7 each added a dedicated clause against exactly that jam and held-out fell every time (0.225 -> 0.1625, 0.15, 0.15), so I did not attack it again. This is instead a strictly lossless compression: 145 vs 153 tokens with every step preserved (differencing ban, index=input, shared affine target, grouping, deg-P root cap, the one-more-forces-P=L tightening, sum-across-the-menu total, block construction). Fewer tokens of identical strategy should transfer at least as well and wins the length tiebreak.

hints.hint: Make each stated condition an equation; pin unknown constants first. Assume nothing unstated. Use the given relation to express remaining unknowns through one variable, then impose the defining equation at every point. Reject roots outside the domain or repeating a known point. A zero or impossible intermediate means relabel, not restart. Box the first candidate meeting every condition.
hints.subagent_summary: Seven of eight rollouts were correct and none ran out of budget. The sole failure pinned the constants correctly, derived the right single-variable equation and the right root, then evaluated the defining relation at that root with a flipped sign and built the last vertex by pure vector arithmetic, never putting either derived point back through the defining equation; it boxed the resulting wrong area. Round 9's instructive failure broke the same way, so this is a twice-observed systematic weakness. The incumbent's unattached "then verify" sits on the constants, which all eight rollouts got right, so it is inert there; those exact tokens are moved into the operative step to name what actually needs checking - the defining equation must hold at every point, derived ones included. All other clauses, including relabel, are kept verbatim, and length is exactly at incumbent parity, 70 tokens.

hints.hint: Model relay-through-a-buffer tasks as stack shunting: fix one labeling, items named bottom-to-top; keep ordered source, buffer and destination stacks. A destination's bottom is whatever arrived first, its top whatever arrived last, so "lands at the bottom" constrains the earliest moves, not the latest. Never assume all n! final orders or runs equally likely: stack rules leave many orders unreachable, forced moves make branches unequal, so a bare 1/k or 1/k! is a red flag. Instead write out a run of moves realizing the event, marking each move forced or free (empty buffer forces a push, empty source a pop; free means both legal). Forced moves cost nothing: count the free moves, and that run's chance is one half to that power. Add over runs if several realize it; check each state's branches sum to one.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts scored 2/8 and the split is clean: both rewarded runs priced the event by writing a run of moves, noticing most moves were forced, counting only the genuinely free binary choices, and taking one half to that count. The six failures never priced a run at all: four substituted a uniform guess (1/24, 1/16, 1/4, 1/2) and two thrashed over reachability until the token limit. A clause grep of all eight shows labeling, forced-move, arrived-first and one-half language present 6-8/8 while 'sum to one', 'red flag' and 'unreachable' appear 1/8, so no clause was cut. The edit changes only the closing directive: the incumbent's abstract 'multiply true per-step probabilities along each admissible word' becomes the concrete move the winners found unaided - write the run, mark each move forced or free, count the free ones, chance is one half to that power - at 176 tokens vs 177.

hints.hint: Numbers before symbols: set the huge parameter to 2, then 3, then 4, solve each tiny integer system by elimination, record the asked value. Divide consecutive entries, tracking signs separately; that ratio exposes the rule. Never build a polynomial in x, never leave the table for theory. Two sizes suffice: scale up and stop.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh round-10 rollouts scored 1/8 and seven emitted no boxed value at all. The failure is not reaching the rule but refusing to accept it: the closest loser derived the correct signed rule from two exact small cases, then burned its remaining budget asking how to derive it ('but how' 30 times, 'must be a mistake' 5 times) and hit the cap; three others computed a correct small-case value, found a half-built theory disagreeing, declared their own arithmetic mistaken, and abandoned the table. The lone winner was the only rollout that accepted its two-size pattern and stopped. The incumbent's closing 'Confirm on one more size, then commit' feeds this: no rollout ever attempts a fourth size, and 'commit' is too vague to license stopping. I keep every clause the winner used verbatim and swap only that closing for an explicit sufficiency-plus-stop rule, at the same 70 tokens.

hints.hint:
Write the quantity asked for as a formula in named symbols, including any unknown the problem never states outright, most often a count. Mark each given number as a total for a group or an amount per item.

If per-item amounts must be whole or equal, that unknown count divides every such total at once, so the candidates are the divisors of their gcd. A count the problem does state describes a grouping; it constrains the unknown count without being it.

Make each percent or ratio a multiplier on the base it acts on, then check the result against every stated condition.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh round-10 rollouts scored 7/8. All eight ran the gcd/divisor machinery and the lone failure was again a selection pick among candidates it had already listed - a fork I tried to patch in rounds 2, 4, 6 and 7 and lost held-out every time, so I left it alone. New evidence: every one of the eight summed the stage totals numerically in its opening paragraph and none introduced a symbol before arithmetic, so 'substitute numbers only at the end' is text the student never executes. This is a single-clause deletion of that inert phrase with every load-bearing move kept verbatim: no rule, prohibition, tiebreak or paraphrase added. 116 tokens versus 123, and my only two wins for this hint (rounds 3 and 5) were evidence-backed deletions.

hints.hint: An identity holding for every x is a symmetry statement, not a coefficient exercise; expanding the composition burns your budget. For p(q(x)) = q(p(x)) take the ansatz p + q = s, s = p(0) + q(0); it collapses the identity to one condition, p(s - x) = s - p(x). Do not solve for coefficients. That relation yields values three ways: it trades an unknown argument for a known one, p(a) = s - p(s - a); q = s - p moves between the maps; the center is fixed, p(s/2) = s/2. Chain these from the given inputs until each requested value appears, then box it.
hints.subagent_summary: 0/8 this round: every rollout hit the 16384-token cap with nothing boxed. All eight adopted the symmetry ansatz, so that part works, but the incumbent's 'read the requested outputs straight from the symmetry relation' says what to achieve without naming any operation, so each fell back to solving for the cubic's coefficients, produced fractional or contradictory ones, and looped ('contradiction' 1-21 times per rollout, two concluding no such polynomials exist). This replaces that inert directive with the three concrete evaluation moves the relation actually supplies - reflect an unknown argument onto a known one, swap maps via q = s - p, and use the center as a fixed point - so values are obtainable with no coefficients at all. These moves are generic to any point-symmetry functional equation, and it is shorter than the incumbent (148 vs 152 tokens).

hints.hint: One application means the whole prescribed sequence of steps, never a single step; settle that first. Run it literally on the smallest nontrivial instance with distinct labels, writing out each state until the original returns, and count. Build a table of the parameter against the measured count and fill three rows the same way before attempting any general argument. A composite does not inherit the period of its parts. Then fit one formula to the table, check it reproduces every row, and box it rather than listing rivals.
hints.subagent_summary: Six of eight rollouts (1/8 correct) hit the 16384-token cap: after measuring only the single smallest case they jumped to an open-ended symbolic composite-permutation argument and spent thousands of tokens re-litigating their own contradictory cycle bookkeeping, never boxing anything; the one success simply measured two sizes and generalized. The incumbent's 'convention slipped' sentence appears in none of the eight traces, and 'get one more size the same way' is too vague to hold them there, so both are replaced by one concrete, countable gate - three measured rows in a parameter-versus-count table before any general argument, then one formula checked against every row. This is shorter than the incumbent and should transfer to any 'in terms of n' question by forcing data collection to finish before abstraction starts.
